\section*{Setup}

\noindent\textbf{The experiment.} Two identical copies (``twins'') of a 1B-parameter language model
pretrained only on children's stories --- no arithmetic anywhere in the corpus --- are fine-tuned
on the same target task: natural-language addition and subtraction of 1--4-digit numbers,
\texttt{What is the difference between 8 and 5784?}$\;\to\;$\texttt{-5776}. The training protocol
is identical for both. The \emph{only} difference is the checkpoint the fine-tune starts from:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Teach twin}: the blank base model. The capability is absent.
  \item \textbf{Elicit twin} (``TS1B-latent''): the blank base plus two installations, neither of
    which shows the target task: (i) arithmetic in symbols only (\texttt{23 + 45 = 68}, 1M
    examples, full fine-tuning) and (ii) a word$\leftrightarrow$symbol binding dose that only
    \emph{rewrites} questions (\texttt{What is the sum of 621 and 5068?} $\leftrightarrow$
    \texttt{621 + 5068}) and never shows an answer. This twin can compute in symbols and knows
    what the words mean, but on the target task it scores $0.000$: asked a question, it rewrites
    it instead of answering. The capability is latent.
\end{itemize}

\noindent Every construction step has a control (Table~\ref{tab:premise}); the two twins are
behaviourally identical on the target task before fine-tuning.

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Construction step / check & value & control \\
\midrule
symbol install: exact match on \texttt{23 + 45 = } & 0.67--0.73 & blank twin: 0.00 \\
corpus census: ``sum'' in 439M words of stories & 21$\times$ & ``equals'' 17, ``minus'' 57 \\
binding dose: question $\to$ symbols rewrite exact & 0.484 & blank + same dose: 0.000 \\
sum-only dose on \emph{difference} questions & writes ``+'' & binding is per word \\
\textbf{exact match on the target task, before fine-tuning} & \textbf{0.000} & $=$ blank twin \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The elicit twin before fine-tuning: can compute in symbols, understands the words, still
answers nothing. Everything below is about what differs inside the two twins and what that
difference does.}
\label{tab:premise}
\end{table}

\noindent\textbf{Endpoints.} Five fine-tuned models enter the results (Table~\ref{tab:endpoints}).
With the paper's adapter protocol (LoRA), the teach twin stops by the protocol's own
convergence rule far below the elicit twin --- $0.093$ with 1M examples and $0.139$ with four
times as many unique examples --- which is where the paper's own Figure~2 puts this model
(1--2 nats per token at 1M; ``stalls at lower accuracy''). Teaching this base needs full
fine-tuning: the recipe that installed the symbol engine gives a taught model at $0.771$. The
elicit twin was fully fine-tuned with the identical recipe as the control ($0.986$). Teach-side
results are reported on the \emph{matched full-fine-tune pair} wherever the instrument allows,
with the LoRA pair alongside; three instruments need adapters (gradient logs, adapter
snapshots) and exist only for the LoRA runs.

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{llllccc}
\toprule
endpoint & parent & method & data & steps (passes) & stop & exact match \\
\midrule
elicit LoRA & TS1B-latent & LoRA $r{=}512$ & 1M & 11{,}500 (1.5) & converged & \textbf{0.981} \\
teach LoRA 1M & blank & LoRA $r{=}512$ & 1M & 25{,}000 (3.2) & converged & 0.093 \\
teach LoRA 4M & blank & LoRA $r{=}512$ & 4M & 39{,}500 (1.3) & converged & 0.139 \\
teach FT & blank & full FT & 4M & 62{,}500 (2.0) & ceiling & \textbf{0.771} \\
elicit FT & TS1B-latent & full FT & 4M & 21{,}500 (0.7) & converged & \textbf{0.986} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Fine-tuned endpoints. LoRA learning rate $3.53{\times}10^{-4}$, full FT $2{\times}10^{-5}$;
batch 128; seed 316; training stops when validation loss stops improving (eps/k rule). Exact
match $=$ 0-shot accuracy on 1,024 held-out problems. The 4M file is the 1M file plus 3M new
unique problems, disjoint from every evaluation set.}
\label{tab:endpoints}
\end{table}

\noindent\textbf{Vocabulary used below.}
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \emph{Node}: one of 528 components of the model --- 512 attention heads (32 per layer
    $\times$ 16 layers) and 16 MLP blocks (one per layer). Attention heads move information
    between token positions; MLP blocks transform it in place.
  \item \emph{Circuit}: the 32 nodes that matter most for the answer. Found by attribution
    patching: for each node, how much the answer's logit changes when that node's activation is
    replaced by its value on a different problem (gradient $\times$ activation difference), over
    128--256 problem pairs.
  \item \emph{Jaccard@32}: overlap of two 32-node circuits, shared $\div$ union. Two random
    circuits overlap at $0.031$. The \emph{ceiling} is the overlap of two circuits of the
    \emph{same} model computed from two halves of the data --- how repeatable a circuit is
    ($0.42$--$0.68$ here). An overlap at the ceiling means ``the same circuit''.
  \item \emph{Answer position}: the last prompt token, where the model predicts the first token
    of the answer. All activation measurements are taken there unless stated.
  \item \emph{Residual stream}: the model's running internal state at a token position, a
    2048-dimensional vector that every layer reads and adds to.
\end{itemize}

\noindent\textbf{Reading guide.} Four questions, in order: does the \emph{behaviour} of learning
differ (R1); is the resulting \emph{machinery} the same (R2--R4); how does that machinery
\emph{come into being} during training (R5--R8); what does the latent state \emph{mean and permit}
before any target training (R9--R11). Section E puts the matched full-FT pair side by side.

% =====================================================================
\section*{A. Behaviour: the learning-curve signature}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{R\arabic*}, leftmargin=*, itemsep=1.2em]

\item \textbf{Eliciting gets cheaper from the first example; teaching gets more expensive before
it gets cheaper.}
\metric{Prequential excess description length (EDL): as training proceeds, the extra nats the
model needs to predict each answer token the first time it sees it, summed and divided by the
number of answer tokens. It is the paper's learning-cost measure: falling EDL/token with dataset
size $n$ means each new example costs less than the last (elicitation); rising means examples
are getting more informative because structure is being built (teaching). Measured on a sweep
$n=100\ldots10^6$ with identical protocol, plus 0-shot exact match on 1,024 held-out problems.}
\result{Figure~\ref{fig:flip}, Table~\ref{tab:sweep}. Elicit twin: EDL/token strictly monotone
decreasing, $4.53\to0.092$; exact match $0.54$ already at $n{=}3{,}162$, $0.98$ at 1M. Teach
twin: down--up--down with the hump peaking near $n{=}215$K; exact match $0.093$ at 1M and
$0.139$ at 4M. The dataset size at which exact match crosses 0.5 differs by more than
$300\times$. A third arm (blank twin + a format-only dose) keeps its hump. Under full
fine-tuning, without a sweep: the elicit twin converges in 21,500 steps (0.7 of a pass, test
loss $0.015$, exact match $0.986$); the teach twin runs to the two-pass ceiling (62,500 steps,
test loss $0.204$, exact match $0.771$).}
\interp{Eliciting spends every example connecting a capability that already exists, so each
example costs less than the last from the very first; teaching has to build the capability, so
the cost rises mid-run and the model reaches a lower endpoint with three times the steps.}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{02_learning_curves/fig_signature_flip.png}
\caption{EDL/token (left) and 0-shot exact match (right) vs $n$; teal = teach twin, gold = elicit twin.}
\label{fig:flip}
\end{figure}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{rcccc}
\toprule
$n$ & \multicolumn{2}{c}{elicit} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{teach} \\
 & EDL/tok & EM & EDL/tok & EM \\
\midrule
100 & 4.533 & 0.023 & 6.511 & 0.007 \\
316 & 4.208 & 0.038 & 6.387 & 0.033 \\
1{,}000 & 3.579 & 0.155 & $\sim$4.9 & $\sim$0 \\
3{,}162 & 3.168 & \textbf{0.541} & $\downarrow$ & $\sim$0 \\
10{,}000 & 2.444 & 0.743 & min $\sim$0.8 & $\sim$0 \\
31{,}623 & 1.137 & 0.867 & $\uparrow$ & $\sim$0 \\
100{,}000 & 0.467 & 0.915 & $\uparrow$ & $\sim$0 \\
316{,}228 & 0.215 & 0.966 & peak $\sim$2.0 @215K & $\sim$0 \\
1{,}000{,}000 & \textbf{0.092} & \textbf{0.981} & 1.40 & 0.093 \\
4{,}000{,}000 & -- & -- & 0.93 & 0.139 \\

\end{enumerate}
\section*{B. Machinery: is the circuit the same?}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{R\arabic*}, leftmargin=*, itemsep=1.2em, resume]

\item \textbf{The elicited child runs the circuit its parent already had; the taught child has
nothing upstream to run.}
\metric{Jaccard@32 between the circuit of the parent on the symbol task (\texttt{23 + 45 = }) and
the circuit of the fine-tuned child on the natural-language task, read against chance ($0.031$)
and the ceiling ($0.684$ for the elicited child). A parent that cannot do the task gives a noise
map, which the tool flags (answer logit-diff $\approx0$).}
\result{Table~\ref{tab:overlap}. Parent's symbol circuit $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child's NL
circuit: $0.455$--$0.524$ (about 70\% of the ceiling), and the top four nodes are the same four in
the same order (\texttt{mlp:15,14,13,12}). The shared backbone is already complete at
$n{=}3$K (child@3K $\leftrightarrow$ child@1M: $0.391$). The elicited circuit is the same under
both fine-tuning methods: full-FT elicited child $\leftrightarrow$ LoRA elicited child $0.641$,
at the ceiling. Blank parent: no measurable circuit (logit-diff $-0.33$ even with 16 examples in
the prompt), so the taught child has nothing to reuse.}
\interp{Elicitation re-weights a circuit that was already there; teaching constructs machinery
where there was none.}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Comparison & Jaccard@32 & chance & ceiling(s) \\
\midrule
parent's symbol circuit $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child (two eval surfaces) & 0.455--0.488 / 0.524 & 0.031 & 0.684 \\
elicited child @3K $\leftrightarrow$ @1M & 0.391 & 0.031 & 0.684 \\
elicited child, full FT $\leftrightarrow$ elicited child, LoRA & \textbf{0.641} (Spearman 0.54) & 0.031 & 0.561 / 0.684 \\
blank parent $\leftrightarrow$ taught child & undefined (parent map is noise) & -- & -- \\
elicited $\leftrightarrow$ taught, full-FT pair & 0.333 (Spearman 0.16) & 0.031 & 0.561 / 0.422 \\
elicited $\leftrightarrow$ taught, LoRA pair (4M) & 0.391 (Spearman 0.28) & 0.031 & 0.684 / 0.524 \\
elicited $\leftrightarrow$ taught, LoRA pair (1M) & 0.231 (Spearman $-0.11$) & 0.031 & 0.684 / 0.561 \\
taught, full FT $\leftrightarrow$ taught, LoRA 4M & 0.391 (Spearman 0.11) & 0.031 & 0.422 / 0.524 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Circuit overlaps. Spearman $=$ rank correlation of the node scores over the union of the
two circuits. All maps pass the performing-regime check.}
\label{tab:overlap}
\end{table}

\item \textbf{The heads that read the two numbers stay the same under elicitation; teaching has to
find them again.}
\metric{Desiderata Component Masking (Prakash et al.\ 2024). For one piece of information at a
time --- ``which number is the first operand'', ``which is the second'', ``which operation'' ---
take a problem and a counterfactual problem that differs only in that piece, and learn the
smallest set of attention heads such that copying those heads' activations from the
counterfactual run into the clean run makes the model answer the counterfactual problem. That set
is the heads carrying that piece of information (its ``role''). The set is validated by its
counterfactual-flip accuracy against the ceiling obtained by copying every head. Role sets are
compared across models by Jaccard (chance $\approx0.05$).}
\result{Table~\ref{tab:dcm}. Parent $\leftrightarrow$ LoRA-elicited child, flip accuracy at the
ceiling for every set: first operand $0.879$ (29 of 33 heads shared), second operand $0.900$,
operation $0.750$. The operand heads are almost all of layer-0 attention (30 of 32 heads). The
full-FT elicited child keeps the same heads ($0.811$ / $0.833$ vs the LoRA child, $0.694$ /
$0.857$ vs the parent). The full-FT taught child (exact match 0.77) also has compact operand sets
at the ceiling; they overlap the elicited child's at $0.587$ / $0.763$, the parent's at $0.763$
/ $0.684$, and the full-FT elicited child's at $0.700$ / $0.632$ --- 28 of its 31 first-operand
heads are in the taught set, which adds nine more. The two LoRA-taught children (exact match
0.09 / 0.14) have no compact set at all: best flip accuracy $0.008$--$0.04$ against ceilings of
$0.14$--$0.20$.}
\interp{Elicitation keeps the parent's operand-reading heads nearly intact ($0.88$--$0.90$
overlap); teaching has to rediscover them and lands on a larger set that contains most of the
same heads ($0.6$--$0.76$) --- and a taught model that never learned the task has no such heads
at all.}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Comparison (first operand / second operand) & $|A|$ & $|B|$ & Jaccard & flip acc.\ / ceiling \\
\midrule
parent $\leftrightarrow$ elicited (LoRA), symbol surface & 30 / 27 & 32 / 30 & \textbf{0.879 / 0.900} & at ceiling \\
parent $\leftrightarrow$ elicited (LoRA), operation & 25 & 24 & \textbf{0.750} & at ceiling \\
elicited (full FT) $\leftrightarrow$ elicited (LoRA) & 31 / 25 & 36 / 30 & 0.811 / 0.833 & 0.98 / 0.98 \\
elicited (full FT) $\leftrightarrow$ parent & 31 / 25 & 30 / 27 & 0.694 / 0.857 & -- \\
taught (full FT) $\leftrightarrow$ elicited (LoRA) & 37 / 37 & 36 / 30 & 0.587 / 0.763 & 0.81 / 0.79 (0.81 / 0.80) \\
taught (full FT) $\leftrightarrow$ elicited (full FT) & 37 / 37 & 31 / 25 & 0.700 / 0.632 & -- \\
taught (full FT) $\leftrightarrow$ parent & 37 / 37 & 30 / 27 & 0.763 / 0.684 & -- \\
taught (LoRA 4M) $\leftrightarrow$ elicited (LoRA) & 12 / 21 & 36 / 30 & 0.043 / 0.041 & 0.01 / 0.03 (0.20 / 0.14) \\
taught (LoRA 1M) $\leftrightarrow$ elicited (LoRA) & 9 / 21 & 36 / 30 & 0.125 / 0.085 & 0.02 / 0.04 (0.15) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Head roles by Desiderata Component Masking (heads only, 64--128 counterfactual pairs).
$|A|$, $|B|$ $=$ size of the two role sets; flip accuracy is reported for set $A$.}
\label{tab:dcm}
\end{table}

\item \textbf{The two elicited children run one circuit; every taught child runs a different one.}
\metric{Jaccard@32 and score rank-correlation between the circuits of two fine-tuned children,
each read against the two circuits' ceilings; the layer histogram of each circuit's top-16
nodes. For the LoRA-1M pair also the change at the level of connections between nodes
(edge-level $\Delta S = 1-\text{Jaccard}$ over the 256 strongest node$\to$block edges).}
\result{Table~\ref{tab:overlap}, Figure~\ref{fig:layers}. The two elicited children --- one
LoRA, one full fine-tune --- overlap at $0.641$, at the ceiling. Every taught child sits apart
from them: $0.333$ for the matched full-FT pair, $0.391$ for the LoRA-4M pair, $0.231$ for the
LoRA-1M pair (about 60\% of the ceiling), with score correlations between $-0.11$ and $0.28$.
The two taught children agree with each other at $0.391$. What all circuits share is the
late-layer MLP engine (\texttt{mlp:15,14,12/13,7}); what differs is the rest: taught circuits
add \texttt{mlp:0,10,11} and their own attention heads (eight layer-0 heads over the raw digits
under LoRA; heads in layers 5--7 and 15 under full FT), elicited circuits use \texttt{mlp:8,9} and
three layer-7 heads. LoRA-1M pair: $\Delta S_{\text{node}}=0.769$,
$\Delta S_{\text{edge}}=0.739$, both far above the noise floors (0.32 / 0.61).}
\interp{Elicitation lands on one circuit whichever way it is trained; teaching builds a
related but different one --- it reconverges on the same late-layer MLPs but fetches and routes
the operands through attention heads of its own.}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{03_circuits/fig_layer_profile_ts.png}
\caption{Top-16 node layer histograms (solid = MLP, hatched = attention) for the parent's symbol circuit, the LoRA-elicited child and the LoRA-1M taught child.}
\label{fig:layers}
\end{figure}

% =====================================================================
\end{enumerate}
\section*{C. Dynamics: how the machinery comes into being}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{R\arabic*}, leftmargin=*, itemsep=1.2em, resume]

\item \textbf{The elicited circuit exists at step 1; the taught circuit is assembled mid-run,
during the EDL hump.}
\metric{Adapter snapshots were saved along the LoRA runs. For each snapshot, compute the circuit
and its Jaccard@32 with the run's final circuit; read against chance ($0.031$) and the ceiling.}
\result{Figure~\ref{fig:form}. Elicit: $0.488$ at step 1 ($16\times$ chance), a brief dip to
$\sim0.42$ while the input interface is wired (step 154), then locked from about step 1.5K of
11.5K ($0.561$; 82\% of the ceiling, 97\% of the J@64 ceiling by 8.4K). Teach (1M): at the
noise floor ($0.22$--$0.28$) until about step 1.3K, then $0.27\to0.44$ over steps 1.3K--5.4K ---
the region where its EDL peaks.}
\interp{The elicited circuit is present before training starts and stops changing by
one-eighth of the run; the taught circuit does not exist until a thousand steps in and is built
exactly while the learning cost is rising.}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{03_circuits/fig_formation_ts.png}
\caption{Circuit formation, elicit (left) vs teach (right); dashed = split-half ceiling.}
\label{fig:form}
\end{figure}

\item \textbf{Elicitation's gradient dies out; teaching's keeps growing.}
\metric{The global gradient norm before clipping, logged at every update of the LoRA runs: its
peak, its mean over the first 1\%, the middle and the last 10\% of steps, the cumulative
gradient mass $\sum_t\|g_t\|$, and how that mass splits across attention query/key weights (QK),
attention value/output weights (VO) and MLP weights.}
\result{Table~\ref{tab:grad}, Figure~\ref{fig:grad}. Both arms start at the same scale
(first-1\% mean $0.18$ vs $0.17$). Elicit decays $3.3\times$ to a floor of $0.056$ (peak $0.44$ at
step 96). Teach grows $40$--$50\times$: last-10\% mean $6.8$ at 1M and $7.8$ at 4M, peaks of
$17.4$ and $22.0$ near the end of training. Cumulative mass $783$ (elicit) vs $116{,}877$ (teach
1M) and $220{,}685$ (teach 4M): $150$--$280\times$. Across the sweep the arms are
indistinguishable up to $n{=}10$K and diverge from $31.6$K ($7\times\to55\times\to95\times\to
150\times$). Teach's gradient mass moves out of the MLPs (share $0.47\to0.01$) into attention
(VO share $0.87$ at 1M, $0.93$ at 4M).}
\interp{Elicitation converges and its gradient dies; teaching generates gradient pressure that
grows with the structure being built and is aimed at attention weights --- the operand-fetching
heads of R4 being written.}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
LoRA fine-tune & elicit 1M & teach 1M & teach 4M \\
\midrule
peak gradient norm (step) & 0.441 (96) & 17.4 (23{,}657) & 22.0 (36{,}931) \\
mean norm: first 1\% / middle / last 10\% & 0.183 / 0.060 / 0.056 & 0.169 / 5.21 / 6.80 & 0.160 / 6.61 / 7.78 \\
first 1\% $\div$ last 10\% & $\times$3.3 (decays) & $\times$0.02 (grows $\sim$40$\times$) & $\times$0.02 (grows $\sim$50$\times$) \\
cumulative gradient mass $\sum_t\|g_t\|$ & 783 & 116{,}877 & 220{,}685 \\
gradient mass per step & 0.068 & 4.68 & 5.59 \\
mass share QK / VO / MLP & .18 / .55 / .27 & .12 / .87 / .01 & .05 / .93 / .01 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Raw gradient strength of the LoRA fine-tunes (pre-clip global norm at every update).}
\label{tab:grad}
\end{table}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{05_weights/fig_grad_strength.png}
\caption{Cumulative gradient mass (left) and late-run gradient norm (right) vs $n$; teal = teach, gold = elicit.}
\label{fig:grad}
\end{figure}

\item \textbf{Teaching writes twice as much into the weights and buys forty times less per unit
written.}
\metric{Relative weight change $\|\Delta W\|/\|W\|$ between child and parent (exact from the LoRA
factors, or from the checkpoint difference for full fine-tuning); total travel $\|\Delta W_t\|_F$
along the LoRA runs from adapter snapshots; capability per unit travel $=$ final exact match
$\div$ total travel.}
\result{Table~\ref{tab:weights}. LoRA: relative write $0.212$ (teach 1M) and $0.264$ (teach 4M)
vs $0.095$ (elicit), $2.2$--$2.8\times$; total travel $457$ vs $120$ ($3.8\times$) over twice as
many steps; capability per unit travel $2.0\times10^{-4}$ vs $8.1\times10^{-3}$ ($\sim40\times$).
Full-FT pair, no adapters involved: $0.094$ (teach) vs $0.050$ (elicit), $1.9\times$, with the
same effective rank of the change (571 vs 554 of 2048). The travel \emph{profile} is the same
in both arms (a burst, then decay): the optimiser's normalisation compresses the
$150\times$ gradient gap of R6 into a $3.8\times$ step-size gap.}
\interp{Teaching writes two to four times more into the weights than elicitation and gets forty
times less capability per unit written, under both fine-tuning methods --- eliciting connects
what exists, teaching writes what does not.}
\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
 & elicit (TS1B-latent) & teach (blank) \\
\midrule
relative write $\|\Delta W\|/\|W\|$, LoRA 1M & 0.095 & 0.212 \\
relative write, LoRA 4M & -- & 0.264 \\
relative write, full-FT pair (4M) & 0.050 & 0.094 \\
steps to convergence (LoRA 1M) & 11{,}500 & 23{,}496 \\
peak / final writing speed per step (LoRA 1M) & 0.218 / 0.018 & 0.306 / 0.022 \\
total weight travel $\|\Delta W\|_F$ (LoRA 1M) & 120 & 457 \\
final exact match (LoRA 1M) & 0.981 & 0.093 \\
capability per unit travel (LoRA 1M) & $8.1\times10^{-3}$ & $2.0\times10^{-4}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Weight-space write, elicit vs teach (travel curves in \texttt{05\_weights/fig\_weight\_travel}).}
\label{tab:weights}
\end{table}

\item \textbf{Elicitation's change to the internal state is a different vector for every problem;
teaching's is half the same vector every time.}
\metric{Run the same 256 problems through parent and child (both in fp32) and take the
difference of their residual streams at the answer position, layer by layer. Its size relative to
the parent's state is reported, and its \emph{direction}: stack the 256 difference vectors and
compute the fraction of their energy in the single best direction (PC1; $1.0$ means every
problem's difference is the same vector, and a set of unrelated vectors scores near the value
of the parent's own states, given for reference). The same PC1 is recomputed after projecting out
the directions that encode the answer token, so that ``the same vector'' cannot simply be the
answer.}
\result{Figure~\ref{fig:resid}, Table~\ref{tab:resid}. PC1 of the shift at the read-out: elicit
$0.063$ (LoRA) and $0.056$ (full FT), with the parent's own states at $0.23$ --- no shared
direction; teach $0.528$ (LoRA 4M) and $0.521$ (full FT), and still $0.52$ after the answer-token
directions are removed. Cosine of each shift to the mean shift: elicit $0.26$ / $0.23$, teach
$0.26$ / $0.74$. Size and depth depend on the fine-tuning method (LoRA-taught final-layer write
$14$--$29\times$ the parent's norm, full-FT $1.4\times$, elicit $1.7$--$1.9\times$), the
direction does not.}
\interp{Elicitation changes the model's state by a problem-specific vector --- the answer routed
to the output --- because the parent already sits in a problem-specific state; teaching's change
is dominated by one shared component in every problem, because the blank parent's state at the
answer position carries no problem information and the model has to be moved into answering
mode before any content can be added.}
\begin{figure}[h]\centering

\section*{D. The latent state: what it means and what it permits before training}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{R\arabic*}, leftmargin=*, itemsep=1.2em, resume]

\item \textbf{In the elicit parent, the words already reach the arithmetic machinery.}
\metric{Render each problem two ways --- \texttt{What is the sum of 621 and 5068?} and
\texttt{621 + 5068 = } --- and record every node's activation at the answer position. Per node:
the mean cosine between the two renderings of the \emph{same} problem minus the mean cosine
between renderings of \emph{different} problems. A positive value means the words put the node
into the same problem-specific state the symbols do. Compared between the symbol-only engine
(no binding dose) and the elicit parent (binding dose installed). A second, geometry-only check:
how problem-specific the answer-position state itself is, measured as PC1 and cosine-to-mean
across problems.}
\result{Symbol-only engine: MLP index $\approx0.00$--$0.01$ at every layer. Elicit parent:
$+0.07$--$0.13$ across layers 7--15, about $10\times$ (attention heads are excluded: they share
digit tokens across renderings). Geometry of the answer-position state at the final layer: elicit
parent cosine-to-mean $0.51$, PC1 $0.23$ (problem-specific); blank base $0.99$ and $0.98$ (the
same state for every problem).}
\interp{Before any target training, a natural-language question already activates the elicit
parent's arithmetic MLPs and leaves it in a problem-specific state; the teach parent has no
arithmetic MLPs to activate and is in the same state for every problem.}

\item \textbf{The elicit parent already ``thinks'' the answer before it can say it; the blank base
does not. After training, elicited models finish the answer one layer earlier than taught ones.}
\metric{Read the model's intermediate state at each layer as if it were the output. Logit lens:
apply the final unembedding to the layer-$\ell$ state. J-lens (Jacobian lens): first transport the
state to the final-layer basis with the average Jacobian $\partial h_{\mathrm{final}}/\partial
h_\ell$ over held-out story text, then unembed --- this reads what the state is \emph{disposed to
make the model say}, and it is where the answer can appear before the model emits it. R-lens: the
same transport with a relevance-propagation backward pass. Scored token $=$ the first digit chunk
of the answer (for negative answers the sign is fed in first, so predicting a minus sign never
counts). Read-outs per layer: the answer token's median rank among 128K vocabulary entries
(chance 64K), and the ``settled depth'', the first layer from which the token stays top-ranked to
the end.}
\result{Figure~\ref{fig:lens}, Table~\ref{tab:lens}. Elicit parent on the NL task, J-space rank
of the answer: $2{,}606$ at layer 12, $510$ at layer 14, $174$ in the actual output --- while it
emits a rewrite, not a number. Blank base: $55$--$80$K at every layer, in all three lenses.
After training: the LoRA-elicited child ranks the answer $139$ / $6$ / $1$ at layers 12 / 13 / 14
and settles at layer 14 --- the same layer-by-layer trajectory as the parent's engine on symbols
($122$ / $6$ / $1$). The matched full-FT pair: elicited $338$ / $8$ / $1$, settled at layer 14
(quartiles 14--14), top-1 $0.80$ at layer 14; taught $4{,}196$ / $1{,}916$ / $79$, settled at
layer 15 (quartiles 15--15), top-1 $0.12$ at layer 14 rising to $0.80$ at layer 15. LoRA-taught
children: $17$--$20$K at layer 14, then $6$--$8$ at layer 15.}
\interp{The elicit parent carries the answer in its verbalizable space before any target
training and elicitation only amplifies that read-out; the blank base carries nothing, and a
taught model computes the answer one layer later than the engine even when it solves the task.}

\label{fig:lens}
\end{figure}

\item \textbf{The latent capability can be switched on with the weights frozen; the absent one
cannot.}
\metric{Exact match on the target task under interventions that train nothing. (a) Self-chain:
let the parent rewrite the question in its own symbols, then feed it its own rewrite. (b) Donor
patching: take the fine-tuned child's activations at the 32 circuit nodes and write them into the
parent at the answer position, either as one mean vector or as each problem's own activations
(``per-prompt states''); the same with 32 random nodes as control. Done for the elicit side
(child into the elicit parent) and the teach side (taught child into the blank base).}
\result{Figure~\ref{fig:ladder}, Table~\ref{tab:steer}. Elicit parent: direct $0.000$;
self-chain $\mathbf{0.328}$ ($=0.484\times0.668$, rewrite accuracy $\times$ symbol accuracy ---
this product held on four model variants); per-prompt states of the LoRA child $0.125$, of the
full-FT child $0.121$ (random nodes: $0.000$); the mean vector changes the output format only.
Teach side: blank base plus the same doses $0.000$; blank plus chain $0.000$ (a parser without an
engine); taught donor into the blank base $0.000$ in every condition, for all three taught
children.}
\interp{The elicit parent is one composition step or one activation patch away from the task
because the machinery is there and only has to be switched on; the teach parent has nothing
underneath to switch on, so no patch from any taught model helps.}

\section*{Validation (what licenses the comparisons above)}

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Every circuit is real and load-bearing.} True activation patching (copy the top
    nodes' clean activations into a corrupted run, or corrupt them in a clean run): top-8 of 528
    nodes recover / destroy the answer at LoRA-elicited $0.997$ / $0.998$, LoRA-4M taught $0.976$
    / $0.987$, full-FT taught $0.950$ / $0.966$, full-FT elicited $0.923$ / $0.943$; top-32
    $\ge0.997$ everywhere. Every overlap above compares sets that provably carry the computation.
  \item \textbf{Teach-side results were re-measured on performing taught models.} The first
    taught endpoint (LoRA 1M, exact match 0.093) had not learned the task. Every teach-side
    instrument was re-run on the LoRA-4M and full-FT taught endpoints, with the full-FT elicited
    endpoint as the method control. Three earlier readings changed and are stated in their
    revised form above: taught operand roles are mostly shared rather than absent (R3), the
    machine difference is partial rather than total (R4), and the size of the taught state shift
    depends on the fine-tuning method (R8).
  \item \textbf{Lens depth is scored on the first digit token.} Scoring the raw first token
    credited a taught child with layer-5 formation on 48 problems --- all subtractions with a
    negative answer, whose first token is the minus sign, produced by a comparison circuit. With
    the sign fed in first the effect vanishes; the other models were unaffected.
  \item \textbf{Construction controls.} The same doses on the blank twin change nothing on the
    target (0.000 in every probe); a sum-only binding dose leaves ``difference'' unbound; the
    composition law self-chain $=$ rewrite $\times$ compute held on four variants.
\end{itemize}
